title: Grasping greed: wanting more, and wanting yours
core: All four cover the appetite for having more — usually money, property, or things — beyond what one has or is owed. They differ on three axes: whether the greed is a settled disposition or a live craving, whether it has the power to take from someone, and whether the speaker is condemning. Three are adjectives describing a character; one is a verb describing a single act of wanting. Sorted below from coldest and most excusable to most predatory.
exam_note: The trap is treating all four as interchangeable insults: **acquisitive** can be neutral or even flattering, **covet** needs a specific object owned by someone else, and **rapacious** needs a victim — so a sentence about a harmless collector, a hoarding miser, and a plundering conqueror each admit only one answer.

words.nuance: The only one that can be neutral or complimentary — a firm, a culture, or a mind can be **acquisitive** without insult. It names a settled policy of accumulating rather than a felt hunger, and it has no victim: the acquisitive person buys and keeps, they do not take.

Narrows the appetite to **money** specifically, and to hoarding rather than seizing — the miser counting coins, not the raider. It is a verdict on a whole character: the speaker is saying money has eaten the man, which is why it never applies to a firm or an intellect.

Requires power and a victim — someone has been stripped bare. Where avarice hoards, **rapacious** plunders, so it attaches to those who can actually take: conquerors, creditors, landlords, extractive industries. Purely condemnatory, and the strongest of the group.

The verb, and the only one aimed at a **particular object already owned by someone else** — your neighbour's house, not wealth in general. The desire is inward, sustained, and sinful in flavour; you can covet for years without ever acting. Note the participle flips: a *coveted* prize is enviable, not shameful.
